text:
Interviewer: This is a United States Holocaust Memorial Museum volunteer collection interview with Peter Miller, conducted by Jack Smith on November 19th, 2001 in Silver Spring, Maryland. This interview is part of the museum’s project to interview Holocaust survivors and witnesses who are also volunteers with the museum. This is tape number one, side A. What is your full name?
Interviewee: Peter Miller.
Interviewer: And what name were you born with?
Interviewee: Hans Miller, with a double L.
Interviewer: And where were you born and when were you born?
Interviewee: I was born in Fürth, it’s a city in Bavaria, south Germany, and I was born on September 6th, 1915.
Interviewer: And who were the members of your immediate family?
Interviewee: My father, my mother, then I had a sister. That’s my im — my immediate family.
Interviewer: What was your father’s name?
Interviewee: David.
Interviewer: And your mother’s name?
Interviewee: Meta, M-e-t-a.
Interviewer: And your sister’s name?
Interviewee: Rosi, R-o-s-i.
Interviewer: Was she older or younger than you?
Interviewee: She was one year younger than me.
Interviewer: Tell a — tell me a little bit about your family. How long had they been in Germany, th-the family — a little bit of the family history.
Interviewee: My mother — my mother’s family dates back to a couple of hundred years, and my father was born in Poland. They got married in 1914, I think, and because my mother was German, my father was Polish born, they — for some reason they could not get married in Germany, so they had to go to — th-the near-nearest ci-city outside Germany, which was in Czechoslovakia, and they were born — they were married there. I found this out only much later.
Interviewer: How did your parents meet?
Interviewee: This I don’t really know. I don’t know th —
Interviewer: Cause you said your father was in Poland and your mother was in Germany, I was wondering how they met.
Interviewee: No, my father me — moved to Germany. I guess he go — hm — for what reason I don’t know, but many Polish Jews at that time moved to Germany.
Interviewer: Did you have an extended family of aunts and uncles or grandparents when you were very young?
Interviewee: Yes, I had my — my — my mother’s parents, who — who lived in the same town in Firth, where I lived. My father’s grandparents lived in Poland. I — I think I met them only twice before, they — when they came for a visit, for lengthy visits.
Interviewer: Y-You said your father’s grandparents, you — do you mean your father’s parents?
Interviewee: Yeah, that’s it.
Interviewer: Yeah. And their names? Do you know the names of your family?
Interviewee: My grandfather’s first name was Isaac. My grandmother’s name in Poland I do — I — I forgot. I really don’t know.
Interviewer: And your mother’s parents?
Interviewee: My mother’s father’s name was Samson, S-a-m-s-o-n. And my grandmother’s first name — can’t think of it right now, me —
Interviewer: Okay, that’s okay. What kind of work did your father do?
Interviewee: Ma — ma — my father was businessman wi — he owned a store.
Interviewer: What kind of store was it?
Interviewee: It was a — a — we had two st — we had two stores, a wholesale and a retail store, and the merchandise we had was haberdashery and wo-woolen things.
Interviewer: And what kind of neighborhood did you live in when you were very young? We’re ba — we’re also talking pre-1933 now. What kind of neighborhood? Was it a Jewish neighborhood, or mixed?
Interviewee: It was a mixed neighborhood, it was not a Jewish neighborhood.
Interviewer: Did you live in an apartment or a house?
Interviewee: Yeah, we — we lived in an apartment, but it was a small apartment house which we owned, and the two businesses, the wholesale and retail store were downstairs in the same building.
Interviewer: What was the name of your father’s business?
Interviewee: The name of my father’s business was David Miller, that’s a — that’s a —
Interviewer: Uh-huh, mm-hm. And was your family very religious?
Interviewee: No, we were not. We were members of a Reform synagogue. In Germany it was not called Reform, it was called Liberal, and Liberal was not as liberal as in — as in this — Reform was not as reformed as in America. It was a little less reformed. For instance, men and women were sitting separately in the synagogue, though we had an organ and otherwise when we consider Reformed service. But — but — but the sexes were separated.
Interviewer: And did you observe the hol — the Jewish holidays at home?
Interviewee: Yes, we observed the Jewish holidays. Saturday we did not observe too well, because our store was open, all the stores were open on Saturday.
Interviewer: And what kind of religious training did you have?
Interviewee: I — my religious training was in public school. It was all — in Germany i-it all over like this. You could not choose. Religious education was given to you in — in public school. That — that went for other religions, too. Twice a week a rabbi came to our s — or a cantor came to our school and the different religions were separated in the different classroom for these lessons.
Interviewer: So yo-you went to what we would call a public school, today. What was the name of your school?
Interviewee: First I went to a private elementary school, and later on to — to — to a high school, which is called gymnasium in Germany. I — I got a humanistic education there. So the emphasis was on Latin, Greek and so on. Not only the languages, but also we learned about culture of the old Romans, Greeks and so on. There — the history, geography and all that.
Interviewer: You said you lived in a mixed neighborhood when you were small. Did you have friends who were not Jewish?
Interviewee: Yes, I did. Mo-Most of my friends were Jewish, but I had a number of Christian friends, too.
Interviewer: Did you feel any different than the — than the Christian children did? Was there — were there any problems? Did you s-sense that as a young child?
Interviewee: No, as a child before Hitler came to power, there were no problems wi — of that kind.
Interviewer: Mm-hm.
Interviewee: Had a — a good relationship with all my friends and there was no — no — there were no traces of anti-Semitism.
Interviewer: How would you describe yourself as a young child? Were you dependent on your parents, or were you very independent?
Interviewee: Dependent. The only thing, f-for awhile in my childhood we had — we had a nanny, because my — both of my parents worked in the business and the first four or five years or so of my childhood, I spent more time actually with my nanny than with my mother, because my mother was mos — busy in the store.
Interviewer: Mm-hm. Would you describe your family as a middle class, upper class?
Interviewee: Middle class.
Interviewer: Di-Did you have a car — did they have a car?
Interviewee: No, they — at that time people in Germany — very few people had cars.
Interviewer: Any hobbies?
Interviewee: In my childhood? Mu-Music was my hobby. I started an early age, I had violin lessons when I was six, piano lessons when I was eight or nine, and later on i-in high school I learned the cello and played in the school orchestra.
Interviewer: Mm-hm. And your relationship with your sister?
Interviewee: I think was normal. Was a normal relationship.
Interviewer: Any favorite holidays that you remember?
Interviewee: As I — I guess like in any other country, for children Passover, Hanukah and Purim.
Interviewer: Any particular holiday that re-remains in your mind that you’d want to describe? Any particular holiday that you would want to describe in detail that you remember? Did you celebrate with your extended family?
Interviewee: No, there were no special — I have no special memories in that respect, as far as holidays are concerned.
Interviewer: And were y — was — were your family members political — your parents politically active?
Interviewee: You mean in — in the congregation or in religious respect? No, they were not.
Interviewer: In — in — in Germany itself, though. In the country itself were they politically active? In the con — in the city.
Interviewee: No, I don’t think so. Actually not.
Interviewer: And were they — would you describe them as Zionists, did they talk about Palestine at all?
